body:
Meaning of volcanism

Volcanism includes geological processes associated with the generation, movement and emplacement of magma within or upon the Earth's crust.

A volcano is an opening or volcanic structure through which lava, gases and fragmented volcanic materials may reach the Earth's surface.

Molten rock material beneath the surface is called magma. When it erupts onto the surface, the molten rock is called lava. Magma may contain dissolved gases and solid mineral crystals.

How magma is generated

Although most of the mantle is solid, particular conditions can cause parts of it to melt. Two especially important tectonic mechanisms are decompression melting and the addition of water.

Decompression melting

At divergent boundaries, hot mantle material rises as plates separate. Pressure decreases during its upward movement, allowing some rock to melt without requiring a corresponding increase in temperature.

The resulting basaltic magma contributes to the formation of new oceanic crust at mid-oceanic ridges.

Melting associated with subduction

At subduction zones, minerals within a descending oceanic plate release water into the overlying mantle. Water lowers the melting temperature of mantle rocks, promoting partial melting.

The resulting magma may rise and generate volcanic activity in the overriding plate. This process helps explain the volcanic arcs associated with oceanic-continental and oceanic-oceanic convergence.

Why eruptions differ

The behaviour of a volcanic eruption depends partly on the composition, temperature, viscosity and gas content of its magma.

Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to flow. Relatively fluid basaltic magma can spread over large distances, while more viscous magma tends to resist movement and may trap dissolved gases as they expand.

Gas-rich, viscous magma can generate explosive eruptions. Relatively fluid magma commonly produces gentler lava flows. These are general tendencies rather than absolute rules; basaltic eruptions can also be explosive under suitable conditions.

Major volcanic landforms

TypeCharacteristic featureExample
Shield volcanoBroad, gently sloping structure formed mainly by fluid lavaMauna Loa, Hawaii
Composite volcanoSteeper structure built from repeated lava and fragmental depositsMount Fuji, Japan
Cinder coneRelatively small cone built mainly from loose volcanic fragmentsParicutin, Mexico
Flood basalt provinceExtensive successive lava sheets, commonly erupted through fissuresDeccan Traps, India

A caldera is a large volcanic depression commonly formed when the ground above a magma chamber collapses following substantial magma withdrawal or eruption. It differs from an ordinary volcanic crater, which is generally a smaller depression surrounding a vent.

Intrusive and extrusive activity

Not all magma reaches the Earth's surface. Magma that cools and solidifies underground produces intrusive igneous bodies. Material that erupts and solidifies at the surface produces extrusive volcanic rocks and landforms.

Granite is a common example of an intrusive igneous rock, whereas basalt is a common extrusive igneous rock.

Important intrusive forms include:

  • Dyke: A sheet-like intrusion that cuts across existing rock layers.
  • Sill: A sheet-like intrusion that follows or lies broadly parallel to existing rock layers.
  • Batholith: A very large body of intrusive igneous rock formed at depth.
  • Laccolith: A typically dome-shaped intrusion that pushes overlying rock layers upwards.

Classification by eruptive activity

  • Active volcano: A volcano that is erupting or is regarded as capable of renewed eruption based on its geological activity.
  • Dormant volcano: A volcano that is presently inactive but may erupt again.
  • Extinct volcano: A volcano considered unlikely to erupt again.

These traditional categories are useful for elementary classification, but the distinction between dormant and extinct volcanoes is not always certain because volcanic systems may remain inactive for very long periods.

Volcanism away from plate boundaries

Volcanic activity can also occur within tectonic plates. A volcanic hotspot is a region of persistent magma generation that may produce volcanoes as a plate moves over it.

The Hawaiian Islands are a classic example of intraplate hotspot volcanism. Successive islands and volcanic mountains have developed as the Pacific Plate moved relative to the volcanic source.

Prelims focus

  • Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is molten rock erupted onto the surface.
  • Divergent boundaries promote decompression melting.
  • Subduction introduces water into the overlying mantle and promotes partial melting.
  • Shield volcanoes are generally broad; composite volcanoes commonly have steeper profiles.
  • Dykes cut across rock layers; sills lie broadly parallel to them.
  • Trap: Volcanism is not confined to plate boundaries, as demonstrated by Hawaii.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26, Chapter 3, pp. 23–26; NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19, Chapter 2, pp. 8–9; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Class 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 4, Earthquake and Volcanoes; USGS, Volcanoes, Principal Types of Volcanoes; USGS, Are the Tectonic Plates Floating on Magma?; USGS, This Dynamic Earth, Hotspots. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Volcanism, Eruptive Processes and Volcanic Landforms

body:
Geographical distribution of tectonic activity

Earthquakes and volcanoes are unevenly distributed across the Earth's surface. Their distribution is closely related to the locations of tectonic plate boundaries and, in some regions, intraplate geological processes.

Circum-Pacific Belt

The Circum-Pacific Belt, popularly known as the Pacific Ring of Fire, extends around much of the margin of the Pacific Ocean.

It contains numerous subduction zones, oceanic trenches, volcanic arcs and earthquake-prone regions. It includes the western margins of North and South America and tectonically active regions around Japan, the Philippines, Indonesia and New Zealand.

The concentration of volcanoes and earthquakes is primarily associated with plate convergence and subduction, although transform boundaries also occur within the broader Pacific tectonic belt.

The Ring of Fire is therefore a broad geographical belt of tectonic activity, not a single continuous volcanic structure or one individual plate boundary.

Mediterranean-Himalayan Belt

The Mediterranean-Himalayan Belt, also called the Alpine-Himalayan or Alpide Belt, extends broadly from the Mediterranean region through parts of West Asia towards the Himalayan region and Southeast Asia.

It is associated with complex convergent interactions involving the African, Arabian, Indian and Eurasian plates and several smaller plates.

Major mountain systems and earthquake-prone zones occur along this belt. The Himalayas are predominantly a continental collision mountain system, while parts of the Mediterranean region also experience subduction-related volcanism.

Mid-oceanic ridge systems

Mid-oceanic ridges form extensive submarine zones of divergent plate movement. They are associated with the creation of new oceanic crust, volcanic activity and predominantly shallow earthquakes.

The Mid-Atlantic Ridge and East Pacific Rise are important examples. Most volcanic activity along these spreading centres takes place beneath the ocean surface.

Volcanism in India

Barren Island

Barren Island is a volcanic island in the Andaman Sea, approximately 135 km northeast of Port Blair. It is associated with a subduction-related volcanic arc.

It is a composite volcano containing a caldera and a central volcanic cone. Documented historical eruptions include those of 1991 and 1994–95.

As of 27 November 2026, the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program lists Barren Island as India's only confirmed Holocene volcano. The Holocene is the geological epoch covering approximately the last 11,700 years.

Barren Island is India's well-established historically active magmatic volcano. This distinction should not be confused with mud volcanoes, which release mud, water and gases rather than ordinary magmatic lava.

Deccan Traps

The Deccan Traps represent an enormous ancient volcanic province formed mainly through repeated outpourings of basaltic lava approximately 66 million years ago, near the end of the Cretaceous Period.

Much of this volcanic activity occurred through fissures. Successive lava flows spread over broad areas and solidified into extensive rock layers. Later erosion exposed these layers, producing characteristic stepped landscapes.

The term trap in Deccan Traps refers to the staircase-like appearance of these geological formations.

The principal volcanic activity occurred before the main phase of Himalayan continental collision, while India was moving northwards towards Eurasia.

Gujarat's volcanic geological heritage

The Deccan volcanic province extends beyond the state of Maharashtra. Basalt-dominated volcanic rocks are also exposed in southern Gujarat, Saurashtra and parts of Kachchh.

These volcanic formations provide evidence that large-scale volcanic activity affected western India in the geological past.

Weathering of basaltic parent material has contributed to the formation of black soils in extensive parts of the Deccan region, including parts of Gujarat. Soil formation also depends on climate, drainage, relief and other local conditions.

The presence of ancient volcanic rocks does not establish that a region has a currently active volcano. Likewise, the earthquake-prone character of Kachchh is primarily related to geological faults and tectonic stress, not to ongoing magmatic eruptions.

Connecting Earth's internal structure with surface processes

The Earth's internal heat and the slow deformation of mantle rocks contribute to lithospheric plate movement. The interaction of plates explains many of the planet's largest geological features.

  • Divergence: Plates separate, mantle rises, magma may form through decompression melting, and new oceanic crust develops. Rift valleys, mid-oceanic ridges and shallow earthquakes are characteristic.
  • Subduction: Dense oceanic lithosphere descends beneath another plate. Oceanic trenches, volcanic arcs and earthquakes ranging from shallow to deep may develop.
  • Continental collision: Continental crust becomes shortened, thickened and uplifted, producing mountain systems such as the Himalayas and associated earthquake activity.
  • Transform movement: Plates slide horizontally past one another, generating shear stress and shallow earthquakes without systematic creation or destruction of crust.
  • Intraplate activity: Geological processes within plates can also generate earthquakes or volcanism, as illustrated respectively by Bhuj and the Hawaiian Islands.

These relationships demonstrate why earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain systems are closely connected, while also explaining why they do not always occur together.

Prelims focus

  • The Pacific Ring of Fire is strongly associated with subduction, volcanic arcs and earthquakes.
  • The Himalayan region belongs to the Mediterranean-Himalayan tectonic belt.
  • Barren Island is located in the Andaman Sea and is a subduction-related volcano.
  • The major Deccan flood-basalt eruptions occurred approximately 66 million years ago.
  • Deccan volcanic rocks occur in southern Gujarat, Saurashtra and parts of Kachchh.
  • Trap: Ancient volcanic rocks do not establish present volcanic activity, and significant earthquakes can occur without volcanism.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26, Chapters 3–4, pp. 23–25 and 29–34; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Class 11, 2020 reprint, Chapters 4–5; Smithsonian Institution, Global Volcanism Program, Barren Island, Geological Summary and Eruptive History, and India Volcanoes catalogue; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Deccan Traps at Panchgani and Mahabaleshwar, Tentative List, Justification of Outstanding Universal Value; Geological Survey of India, Briefing Book, Gujarat regional geology section; USGS, This Dynamic Earth, Understanding Plate Motions; USGS, The Mw 7.7 Bhuj Earthquake, 2003. Online sources and volcano catalogue status consulted 27 November 2026.]
